findings.title: Hardcoded Public DNS Resolvers Bypass Enterprise Controls
findings.description: Device sends DNS queries directly to public resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, etc.) instead of using the DHCP-supplied resolver, bypassing enterprise DNS filtering, sinkholing, anomaly detection and split-DNS.
findings.impact: Enterprise DNS controls are bypassed for the device's most security-relevant traffic. Security teams cannot detect or block the device contacting unexpected endpoints, cannot apply DNS-based egress restrictions, and cannot audit data-exfiltration patterns. Represents a HIPAA / SOC 2 logging control gap.
findings.owasp_web: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.remediation_brief: Modify device firmware to use only the DHCP-supplied DNS resolver. Implement DoH/DoT. Provide deployment-time toggle for hospital IT to constrain the resolver.

findings.title: Cleartext DNS Exposes External Service Topology
findings.description: All DNS queries are sent over cleartext UDP/53. Any on-path observer can enumerate the full set of external services the device depends on.
findings.impact: An attacker who can passively observe device traffic learns the entire backend architecture without active probing — cloud-provider endpoints, push-notification dependencies, captive-portal probe destinations and SaaS services in use.
findings.remediation_brief: Implement DNS-over-HTTPS (RFC 8484) or DNS-over-TLS (RFC 7858) on the device.

findings.title: Device Identity Leaked in TLS Client Certificate (mTLS)
findings.description: The device authenticates with a client X.509 certificate (mTLS). The certificate subject is sent in cleartext during the handshake and exposes identifying information (serial, model, vendor PKI topology).
findings.impact: Passive observers can extract the device's identity from the TLS handshake bytes without decrypting any application data. Privacy-relevant in clinical contexts where the presence of a particular medical device indicates the patient population being served.
findings.remediation_brief: Use opaque per-device identifier (UUID) as the Subject CN. Move human-readable serial / model into a custom certificate extension or SubjectAltName otherName.

findings.title: TLS ClientHello Offers Legacy CBC Cipher Suites
findings.description: The device's TLS ClientHello offers legacy CBC-mode cipher suites alongside modern AEAD ciphers. While AEAD is typically negotiated, the CBC offer preserves a downgrade surface.
findings.impact: CBC suites are vulnerable to historical attacks (BEAST, Lucky13, POODLE-variants) when paired with TLS 1.0/1.1. In TLS 1.2 with correct implementation the practical exploit cost is high but the offer is unnecessary given AEAD alternatives are universally supported by every modern endpoint.
findings.remediation_brief: Remove CBC cipher suites from the device's TLS ClientHello offer list. Keep only AEAD: TLS 1.3 (0x1301/02/03) and TLS 1.2 ECDHE-AEAD (0xc02c/2b/30/2f).

findings.title: DHCP Hostname Discloses Asset Identifier
findings.description: The device populates DHCP option 12 (Host Name) with an asset identifier (serial number, device tag) that is broadcast on every DHCP DISCOVER/REQUEST.
findings.impact: Any host on the broadcast domain can passively map the device's MAC and IP to the broadcast asset tag — vendor, model and serial are derivable without sending a single packet. Combined with mDNS reflection this is reflected across L3 boundaries.
findings.remediation_brief: Replace DHCP Host Name with an opaque per-device identifier (UUID or salted hash). The true serial should only travel inside the encrypted device-to-cloud channel.

findings.title: DNS Search-Suffix Appended to Fully-Qualified Hostnames
findings.description: The device's DNS client appends the DHCP-supplied search domain to hostnames that are already fully-qualified. RFC 1535 and RFC 8767 require resolvers not to apply search-suffix processing to FQDNs.
findings.impact: An attacker controlling the search-suffix DNS zone can redirect the device's cloud traffic to attacker-controlled IPs. TLS server certificate validation usually catches the substitution, but the failure mode leaks connection metadata on every retry. If cert pinning is incorrectly implemented, the substitution succeeds.
findings.remediation_brief: Patch device DNS client so hostnames with three or more labels (or trailing dot) bypass search-domain processing. Set 'ndots' threshold to 1.

findings.title: SMBv1 Traffic Observed (EternalBlue / NotPetya exposure)
findings.description: SMBv1 protocol traffic observed between the device and one or more internal peers. SMBv1 is deprecated since 2014 and is the transport for EternalBlue (MS17-010) / WannaCry / NotPetya.
findings.impact: Active SMBv1 on a clinical network creates a worm propagation path. Disable per FDA Postmarket Cybersecurity Guidance and Joint Commission EHR-protection expectations.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable SMBv1 on every host. Confirm SMB2+ minimum on file servers. Block 445/tcp at segmentation boundary.

findings.title: LLMNR / NBT-NS Name Resolution in Use (Responder Surface)
findings.description: LLMNR or NetBIOS Name Service broadcast-based name resolution is in use on the segment. These protocols are abused by Responder / Inveigh to poison name resolution and capture NTLMv2 hashes.
findings.impact: An attacker on the same broadcast domain runs `responder -I eth0` and captures hashes from any device that mistypes a hostname or uses a non-FQDN lookup. Hashes are crackable offline or relayed via ntlmrelayx for immediate authentication elsewhere (CVE-2019-1040 mitigations notwithstanding).
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR (GPO: Turn Off Multicast Name Resolution = Enabled) and NBT-NS (Network adapter → WINS → Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP). Block UDP/5355 and UDP/137 at every L3 boundary.

findings.title: SSDP / UPnP Broadcasts Expose Internal Services
findings.description: SSDP/UPnP discovery traffic observed on the segment. SSDP advertises every UPnP-aware device (smart TVs, consumer routers, printers, NAS, IoT) on the local broadcast domain.
findings.impact: SSDP discovery reveals consumer-IoT, printers, smart TVs, NAS and router admin interfaces to anyone on the LAN. In a clinical network this co-mingles consumer devices with medical equipment and facilitates lateral discovery.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable UPnP/SSDP on clinical-network hosts where not required. Block UDP/1900 at every L3 boundary.

findings.title: mDNS Activity Exposes Device Identity on Internal Segment
findings.description: Device emits mDNS queries and/or responses on the local segment. mDNS exposes the device's hostname and services to any host on the multicast-reachable segment, and is reflected across L3 by mDNS-reflector-enabled gateways.
findings.impact: Device fingerprinting and asset enumeration without active probing. Reduces the cost of targeting a specific device for theft, social-engineering, or RF replay attack.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable mDNS on the device if not required. Audit network-side mDNS reflector config (Avahi `reflector=yes`, UniFi 'Multicast DNS') and disable cross-VLAN reflection.

findings.title: LLDP Topology / Switch Firmware Disclosure
findings.description: LLDP TLVs observed on the segment leak switch identity, model and firmware. Information that downstream attackers can use to select vendor-specific CVEs.
findings.impact: An attacker passively learns the network gear vendor, model and firmware version without sending any probes. Combined with public CVE databases this is a free vulnerability-research head-start.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLDP on access ports facing devices (`no lldp transmit` / `no lldp receive`). Keep LLDP only on inter-switch trunks.

findings.title: ARP Anomalies (Duplicate IP-to-MAC Mappings)
findings.description: Duplicate ARP entries observed — one IP advertised by multiple MAC addresses. Possible legitimate HA pair, gratuitous ARP storm, or active ARP-spoofing / MitM.
findings.impact: If the duplicate is a MitM attack, the attacker is intercepting traffic between the device and another host. Even when legitimate (HA failover), the unannounced duplicate breaks deterministic L2 routing and may drop packets.
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate each duplicate. Configure DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection) on managed switches. Bind static IP↔MAC for critical clinical-device subnets.

findings.title: Cleartext FTP Traffic Observed (credentials in plaintext)
findings.description: FTP control-channel traffic observed in cleartext. FTP USER/PASS commands and file contents are passively captureable by any on-path observer.
findings.impact: Any L2 / SPAN / WiFi-sniffing attacker can capture FTP credentials and uploaded/downloaded file content. In a clinical setting this may include device firmware, calibration data, or PHI.
findings.remediation_brief: Disable FTP. Use SFTP (SSH) or FTPS (FTP over TLS, explicit AUTH TLS). Block 21/tcp at segmentation boundary.

findings.title: Cleartext Telnet Traffic Observed
findings.description: Telnet traffic observed in cleartext. Telnet credentials and keystrokes are sent in plaintext and trivially captured by passive observers.
findings.impact: Full session capture — usernames, passwords and every keystroke are recoverable from a passive sniff. Common on legacy embedded and industrial-control devices.
findings.remediation_brief: Replace Telnet with SSH. Block 23/tcp at every L3 boundary.

findings.title: SNMPv1/v2c Community String in Cleartext
findings.description: SNMP community strings (passwords) observed in plaintext. Communities like 'public' / 'private' / vendor-default values grant MIB-table read access (or write if RW).
findings.impact: SNMP community strings are passwords. An attacker capturing them can read MIB data (interface stats, ARP tables, routing tables) and with a write community can reconfigure the device.
findings.remediation_brief: Migrate to SNMPv3 with authentication (SHA) + encryption (AES). Disable SNMPv1/v2c. Restrict SNMP source IPs at the device.

findings.title: HTTP Basic Authentication Observed in Cleartext
findings.description: HTTP Basic Auth headers observed in cleartext. Authorization: Basic <base64> is one base64-decode step away from username:password.
findings.impact: Basic Auth credentials are base64-encoded usernames+passwords. Any passive observer can decode them in one step (`base64 -d`). Often reused across many systems.
findings.remediation_brief: Wrap the affected service in TLS (HTTPS) or replace Basic Auth with token/cookie-based scheme over TLS. Block plain HTTP on authenticated admin endpoints.

findings.title: LDAP Bind Observed Without TLS
findings.description: LDAP bind request observed in cleartext. Without LDAPS or StartTLS, the bind DN and password are exposed.
findings.impact: An attacker capturing the bind can extract the LDAP credentials. Domain-bound accounts are reusable across the AD forest and may unlock additional services (Kerberos, file shares, mail, VPN).
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce LDAPS (TCP/636) or LDAP+StartTLS. Block plain LDAP (389/tcp) at the firewall.
